chunks: This affair has not begun with you,
nor does it end with you,
and your companion has indeed been journeying,
so consider him as still among his journeys,
if he arrives to you, or else you will arrive to him.

key_terms.الْأَمْرَ: The affair/command (referring to Imamate or divine authority)

ai.seo_question: What does Nahj al-Balagha say about the Imam's absence and the nature of his journey?
ai.summary: This narration, often cited in discussions of the Imam's occultation (Ghaybah), underscores that divine authority (al-Amr) transcends temporal human control, belonging ultimately to God and His chosen Imam. It encourages believers to maintain spiritual vigilance and readiness for reunion, whether through the Imam's return or their own pilgrimage to him, reflecting the Shia concept of the Imam as the enduring guide even in his absence. The reference to 'journeying' (yasafaru) is interpreted by scholars as both a physical travel and a metaphor for the Imam's hidden presence among the people.
